grammar.title: Saying what something is — 係
grammar.plain: Cantonese has no “am/is/are” before an adjective, but it needs 係 (hai6) to link two things: 我係加拿大人 — I am a Canadian. With an adjective you use 好 instead: 我好攰 — I am tired.
grammar.watch: Don’t put 係 before an adjective. 我係攰 is wrong; 我好攰 is right.

grammar.title: Saying no — 唔
grammar.plain: 唔 (m4) goes straight in front of the verb: 我唔食 — I don’t eat. It is the everyday “not” for verbs and adjectives.
grammar.watch: For “don’t have” and “didn’t”, Cantonese uses 冇 (mou5), not 唔有.

grammar.title: Something finished — 咗
grammar.plain: 咗 (zo2) sits right after the verb and marks the action as done: 我食咗飯 — I have eaten. It is about completion, not about the past: 聽日食咗飯先 — after eating tomorrow.
grammar.watch: It follows the verb. 我咗食飯 is wrong.

examples.text: Tom 敲咗 Mary 房門。
examples.eng: Tom knocked on the door to Mary's room.
Tom went back to his hometown.

grammar.title: Something in progress — 緊
grammar.plain: 緊 (gan2) after the verb means the action is going on right now: 我食緊飯 — I am eating. Same position as 咗, opposite meaning.
grammar.watch: The corpus of 1990s conversation barely tags 緊 on its own, but it is everywhere in Tatoeba’s sentences and in speech today — a reminder that the corpus is a sample, not the language.

grammar.title: Asking with “have or not” — 有冇
grammar.plain: Cantonese asks questions by offering both options: 你有冇時間？ — do you have time (have, not have)? The pattern works with any verb: 去唔去 — going or not?
grammar.watch: Answer by repeating the verb: 有 or 冇 — not “yes” or “no”.

examples.eng: Do you have a Twitter account?

grammar.title: Asking either way — V唔V
grammar.plain: The same question shape with other verbs: 好唔好？ — is it good? 得唔得？ — will that do? Say the verb, 唔, then the verb again.
grammar.watch: With 係 this becomes 係唔係 — the ordinary way to ask “is it?”

examples.eng: Do you have time the day after tomorrow?

grammar.title: Whose and which — 嘅
grammar.plain: 嘅 (ge3) joins a describer to a thing, like ’s and “that”: 我嘅書 — my book; 佢買嘅嘢 — the thing he bought.
grammar.watch: At the end of a sentence 嘅 does another job: it makes a statement sound settled.

grammar.title: Counting things — 個, 啲, 隻
grammar.plain: A number or “this/that” needs a measure word before the noun. 個 (go3) is the general one: 一個人. 啲 (di1) covers “some” and plurals: 呢啲嘢. 隻 (zek3) is for animals and one of a pair: 一隻狗.
grammar.watch: 個 is the safe default when you don’t know the right measure word — speakers will understand you.

examples.eng: Bring the water to a boil.

grammar.title: The word that carries the attitude — 啊, 喇, 咩, 喎
grammar.plain: Cantonese puts the speaker’s attitude in a particle at the end. 啊/呀 softens. 喇 says something has changed or is settled. 咩 asks in surprise — 真係咩？ really? 喎 passes on what someone else said, or marks it as news.
grammar.watch: These are not decoration. Leaving them off is what makes correct Cantonese sound blunt or foreign.

grammar.title: Back, again, and along — 返, 埋, 住
grammar.plain: Short words after the verb change what it means. 返 (faan1) is back or again: 返屋企 — go home. 埋 (maai4) adds the rest, or joins in: 食埋佢 — finish it. 住 (zyu6) holds the state for now: 等住 — wait (and stay waiting).
grammar.watch: They stack after the verb, before the object.
